# Introduction

While the first data center was opened in 1946[@Tozzi2026], it was not until the 2000s that data centers became common. And it has only been a handful of years since an explosion in both the construction and scale of new data centers due to the widespread adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs). This growth has led to a dramatic increase in data centers’ resource usage and consequent economic influence[@Schulz2025]. Most of the public discourse and recent research on data centers focus on the impacts on energy and water. However, the economic ramifications on the communities surrounding these facilities have received relatively little attention to date.

Research on this topic has been hampered by a lack of data on data centers. This breaks down into two sub-issues: (1) a lack of historical data--a natural consequence of the recent explosion in construction, and (2) a lack of complete and precise information on the timing and scale of specific data center construction. The first issue will resolve itself with time, but the second is a transparency issue systemic to the industry. Several private data aggregators, such as Aterio, Cleanview, and Data Center Map, offer approximations of the temporal and geospatial data required to research the local economic and environmental impacts of data centers, but at prices prohibitive to all but the best-funded labs. Our paper presents a novel approach to resolving this data sourcing and consistency problem, opening the door to future research. 

Resolving these data and consistency bottlenecks is critical not only for empirical research, but also because data centers’ rapid surfacing in the public consciousness has allowed misconceptions to calcify regarding what a 'data center' actually is and how its placement affects local communities. Our analysis clarifies these points by defining data centers strictly as those operations that meet the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) subsector code 518, which is defined as follows: “The Computing Infrastructure Providers, Data Processing, Web Hosting, and Related Services subsector groups establishments that provide computing infrastructure, data processing services, Web hosting services (except software publishing), and related services, including streaming support services (except streaming distribution services)”[@NAICS518]. Using this definition provides several benefits. The first is that it uses a national standard already common in economics literature, making an already extensive body of work based on this system compatible and comparable. The second, and perhaps greater, benefit is that U.S. federal statistics, such as those collected by the Bureau of Labor Statistics and the U.S. Census Bureau, use these codes and report consistent, historical data with them. All other currently available datasets tracking the timing and location of data center construction must invent their own operational definition of “data center” and decide which operations match that definition across hundreds or thousands of regional databases.

This project aims to further this nascent area of research by surveying a broad swath of economic indicators, from residential construction permit counts to average personal income, to uncover relationships between these economic variables and the entrance of data centers over time. In undertaking our survey, we present three contributions to the literature. First, we construct an accessible, open-source time-series pipeline for tracking data center entry over time, resolving key data-access bottlenecks. Second, we apply difference-in-differences (DiD) specifications to benchmark our open data against existing literature and validate local economic effects. Third, we integrate machine learning both as a feature-selection mechanism for our causal DiD models and as an end-to-end predictive framework using Variational Autoencoders (VAEs).
